body_md:
\label{def:ToeplitzMun-EU-tree} Let $E$ be a directed graph and let $U$ be a subset of $E^1$.
 We define a {\it Toeplitz-Munn $(E,U)$-tree} as a pair $(T,g)$ where $T$ is a finite 
		connected subgraph of $\Gamma_E$ containing the root $v$ corresponding to its connected component, and such that all maximal elements of $T$ do not end in $E^{-1}$, and do
		not end in an edge $e\in U$, and  $g= g_U w$ satisfies that $g_U\in T$.

label: lem:uniqueTU
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be an $E$-tree. For each $g\in \mathfrak{F_{gr}} (E)$, we consider its canonical decomposition $g=g_U w$ with respect to $U$ (see Definition \ref{def:canonicaldec-respect-toU}).
	
	Now set $A:= \{ g_U: g\in T\}$, and $T_U = \mathrm{max} (A)^\downarrow $. Then the set of maximal elements of $T_U$ is exactly $\mathrm{max} (A)$, and thus all maximal elements of $T_U$ do not end in $E^{-1}$ and do not end in $U$. Since $T_U\subseteq T$, it follows that $T\le T_U$.
	
	Also, as in the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.16]{ABC25}, we have $T_U\sim_U T$.  
	
	We now want to show that, if $S$ is an $E$-tree and $T\sim_U S$ in $\mathcal M$, then $S_U=T_U$. Let $(T_0,g_0), (T_1,g_1), \dots , (T_n,g_n)$ be a sequence of Munn $E$-trees, with $(T_0,g_0)= (T,1)$ and $(T_n,g_n)= (S,1)$, and such that for each $0\le i < n$, we can pass from $(T_i,g_i)$ to $(T_{i+1},g_{i+1})$, or from $(T_{i+1}, g_{i+1})$ to $(T_i,g_i)$, by a single step either of the form 
	$$(X,h) (\{r(e)\}, r(e))(Y,k) \sim_U
	(X,h) ((e^{-1})^\downarrow , r(e)) (Y,k)$$
	 for $e\in E^1$, or of the form
	$$(X,h) (\{s(e)\}, s(e))(Y,k) \sim_U
(X,h) (e^\downarrow , s(e)) (Y,k)$$	  
	for $e\in U$. 
	
	In both cases, we have $(Z, h\cdot k) \sim_U (Z\cup h\cdot x^\downarrow, h\cdot k)$, where $x\in E^{-1}\cup U$, and  $Z= X\cup h\cdot Y $ is an $E$-tree such that $h\in Z$. It thus suffices to show that in such a situation, one has $Z_U = (Z\cup  h\cdot x^\downarrow)_U$. If $hx$ is not reduced then 
	$h\cdot x\in Z$ and we indeed have $Z=Z\cup  h\cdot x^\downarrow $. If $hx $ is reduced, then $h_U= (hx)_U$ and hence $\{ z_U: z\in Z\} = \{z_U: z\in Z\cup  h\cdot x^\downarrow \}$, showing that 
	$Z_U=  (Z\cup h\cdot x^\downarrow)_U$, as desired. Applying inductively this fact to all the consecutive pairs of elements in the sequence $\{ (T_i,g_i)\}$, we obtain that $T_U=S_U$. Hence $S\le T_U$ for all $S\in [T]_U$,
	and $T_U$ is the largest element of $[T]_U$ in $\mathcal M _U$. Also it is clear from this fact that 
	$T_U$ is the unique element in $[T]_U$ with the property that each maximal element does not end in $E^{-1}\cup U$.

label: prop:Toeplitz-Munn-EUtrees
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Toeplitz-Munn-EUtrees}
	Let $E$ be a directed graph, let $U$ be a subset of $E^1$ and set $\mathcal M_U= \mathcal M/{\sim_U}$. 
	 Then the inverse semigroup $\mathcal M _U$ is isomorphic to the inverse semigroup $\mathcal T_U \mathcal M$ consisting of all the Toeplitz-Munn $(E,U)$-trees $(T,g)$, endowed with the product 
	$$(T_1,g_1)\cdot (T_2,g_2) = \begin{cases} \Big( (T_1'\cup g_1\cdot T_2')_U, \,\, g_1\cdot g_2\Big) & \text{ if } r(g_1) = s(g_2)\\ \qquad \,\,  \qquad \,\, 0 & \text{ if } r(g_1) \ne s(g_2) 
	\end{cases}   $$
	where $T_1',T_2'\in \mathcal E (\mathfrak{F_{is}} (E))$ are representatives of $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively, such that $g_1\in T_1'$ and $g_2\in T_2'$. The inverse is given by  	
	$(T,g)^{-1} = ((g^{-1}\cdot T')_U, g^{-1})$,
	where $T'$ is any representative of $T$ such that $g\in  T'$. 
	
	Moreover, the map $(T,g)\mapsto \omega (g)$ determines an idempotent pure partial homomorphism $\mathcal T_U \mathcal M \to \mathbb F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We define a map $\Phi \colon \mathcal M_U \to \mathcal T_U \mathcal M$ by $\Phi ([T,g]_U) = (T_U, g)$. Note that this map is well-defined since for $(T,g)\in \mathcal M$, we have $g\in T$ by definition, and thus $g_U\in T_U$, and moreover $T_U=S_U$ and $g=h$ whenever $(T,g)\sim_U (S,h)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:cosequenceofuniqueTU}(1). Moreover the map $\Phi$ is injective again by Lemma \ref{lem:cosequenceofuniqueTU}(1). If $(T,g)$ is a Toeplitz-Munn $(E,U)$-tree, then $(T\cup g^\downarrow, g)$ is a Munn $E$-tree, and $\Phi ([T\cup g^\downarrow , g]) = (T,g)$, which shows that $\Phi$ is surjective.
	
	Since $\Phi$ is a bijection, we can translate the product of $\mathcal M _U$ to a product in $\mathcal T_U \mathcal M$, so that $\Phi$ becomes a semigroup isomorphism. This leads to the product described in the statement.
	
	
	Let $\omega \colon \mathfrak{F_{gr}} (E)^\times \to \mathbb F$ be the obvious 
	 idempotent pure partial homomorphism. Then the map
	 $\pi\colon \mathfrak{F_{is}} (E)^\times \to \mathbb F$, $\pi (T,g) = \omega (g)$ is the canonical idempotent pure partial homomorphism of $\mathfrak{F_{is}} (E)\cong \mathcal M$, see \cite[Corollary 4.3]{ABC25}. It is clear that $\pi$ 
	 factors through an idempotent pure partial homomorphism $\mathfrak{F_{is}} (E)^\times /{\sim_U} \to \mathbb F$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Note that if $(T,g)$ is a Toeplitz-Munn $(E,U)$-tree (see Definition \ref{def:ToeplitzMun-EU-tree}), it might be that $(T,g)$ is not a Munn $E$-tree, because it might be that $g\notin T$, although by definition we always have that $g_U\in T$. This means that doing calculations in the inverse semigroup $\mathcal T_U \mathcal M \cong \mathcal T _U(E)$, we must be careful and take representatives $T'$ of $T$ in $\mathcal E (\mathfrak{F_{is}}(E))$ such that $g\in T'$, so that $(T',g)$ is a Munn $E$-tree. We can always do the choice $T'=T\cup g^\downarrow$. We have the formulas 
$$(T,g)(T,g)^{-1} = T,\qquad (T,g)^{-1}(T,g) = (g^{-1}\cdot T \cup \{g^{-1}\}^\downarrow)_U$$
for a Toeplitz-Munn $(E,U)$-tree $(T,g)$.

The corresponding equivalence classes are denoted by $[T,g]_L$, or $[T]_L$ if $T\in \mathcal E (\mathfrak{F_{is}}(E))$.
	
	
	For each $E$-tree $T$, we denote by $T_L$ the unique element $T_U$ described in Lemma \ref{lem:uniqueTU}, where $U$ is the subset of $E^1$ consisting in all edges $e\in E^1$ such that $\{ e \}\in C$. Hence $T_L$ is the unique element of $[T]_L$ such that each maximal element of $T_L$ does not end in $E^{-1}$ and does not end in $e$, for $e\in E^1$ with $\{ e\}\in C$.

label: lem:extesnio-to-CcompatibleEtree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:extesnio-to-CcompatibleEtree}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and let $T$ be a $C$-compatible $E$-tree. Then each $S\in \mathfrak{F_{is}}(E)$
	with $S\sim_L T$ is also $C$-compatible.
		 In particular, if $(T,g)$ is a Leavitt-Munn $(E,C)$-tree, then $T\cup g^\downarrow$ is $C$-compatible, and thus it belongs to $\mathcal X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem:uniqueTU}, it is enough to show that if $T$ is an $E$-tree and $T_L$ is $C$-compatible, then $T$ is also $C$-compatible. 
	
	Let $T$ be an $E$-tree such that $T_L$ is $C$-compatible. Given two vertices $g$ and $h$ in $T$, we have to show that $g^{-1}\cdot h$ is a $C$-separated path. 
	
	We first observe that all elements of $T$ are $C$-separated. Take $g\in T$. By the construction of $T_L$ we have $g_L\in T_L$, so that we can write $g= g_L w$, where $g_L\in T_L$ and $w$ is a product of inverse edges and of edges $e$ such that $\{ e\}\in C$. Since $T_L$ is $C$-compatible, $g_L$ is $C$-separated, and it follows that $g=g_L w$ cannot contain a subword of the form $e^{-1}f$, where $e,f$ are distinct edges in $E$ such that $e,f\in X$ for $X\in C$.
	
	Consider now two vertices $g,h\in T$. If one of them is a prefix of the other, then we deduce from the above that $g^{-1}\cdot h$ is $C$-separated. Hence we may assume that $g= dxg'$ and $h= dyh'$, where $x,y\in E^1\cup E^{-1}$ and $x\ne y$. We need to show that 
	$g^{-1}\cdot h = (g')^{-1} x^{-1}y h'$ is $C$-separated. Since $(g')^{-1}x^{-1}$ and $yh'$ are $C$-separated, we only have to show that $x^{-1}y$ is not of the form $e^{-1}f$ for $e,f$ distinct edges in the same set of the partition $C$. If $dx$ is a prefix of $g_L$ and $dy$ is a prefix of $h_L$, then the above property holds because $g_L,h_L\in T_L$, and $T_L$ is $C$-compatible. If $g_L$ is a proper prefix of $dx$, then either $x\in E^{-1}$ or $x\in E^1$ and $\{x\}\in C$, hence $x^{-1}y$ is not of the form $e^{-1}f$ described above. The same conclusion can be reached if $h_L$ is a proper prefix of $dy$. This completes the proof.

label: thm:ECLeavittMunntrees
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ECLeavittMunntrees}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Then the Leavitt  inverse semigroup $\mathcal{LI} (E,C)$ is isomorphic to the inverse semigroup consisting of all Leavitt-Munn $(E,C)$-trees, endowed with the following product
	$$(T_1,g_1)\cdot (T_2,g_2) = \begin{cases} \Big( (T_1'\cup g_1\cdot T_2')_L, \,\, g_1\cdot g_2\Big) & \text{ if } T_1'\cup g_1\cdot T_2' \text{ is }C\text{-compatible} \\ \qquad \,\,  \qquad \,\, 0 & \text{ otherwise }  
	\end{cases}   $$
	where $T_1',T_2'\in \mathcal X$ are any representatives of $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively, such that $g_1\in T_1'$ and $g_2\in T_2'$.
	The inverse is given $(T,g)^{-1} = ((g^{-1}\cdot T')_L, g^{-1})$, where $T'$ is any representative of $T$ such that $g\in T'$. 
	The map $(T,g)\mapsto \omega (g)$ provides an idempotent pure partial homomorphism $\mathcal{LI}(E,C)^\times \to \mathbb F$, which determines a semidirect product decomposition
	$$\mathcal{LI} (E,C) \cong \mathcal Y^L \rtimes_{\theta}^r \mathbb F,$$
	where $\mathcal Y^L = \mathcal X/{\sim_L}\cong \mathcal E (\mathcal{LI} (E,C))$. The partial action $\theta^L$, with $\theta^L_g\colon D_{g^{-1}}^L\to D_g^L$ is defined as follows:
	For each $g\in \mathbb F_{C}(v)\setminus \{v\}$, $D_g^L$ can be identified with the set of all those $T\in \mathcal X_L(v)$ such that $g_L\in T$, and the action $\theta_g^L$ is defined by $\theta_g^L(T)= (g\cdot T')_L$, where $T'$ is a representative of $T$ containing $g^{-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows the pattern of \cite[proof of Theorem 4.5]{ABC25}. We include details for the convenience of the reader. 
	
	If $S$ is any strongly $E^*$-unitary inverse semigroup with an idempotent pure partial homomorphism $\theta \colon S^\times \to \Gamma$, and $I$ is an ideal of $S$, then $S/I$ is also strongly $E^*$-unitary with the same group $\Gamma$.
	This is clear since $(S/I)^\times$ can be identified with $S\setminus I$, and thus the restriction of $\theta $ to $S\setminus I$ gives the desired idempotent pure partial homomorphism. 
	
	Now let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Since the Leavitt inverse semigroup $\mathcal{LI} (E,C)$ is the Rees quotient of the inverse semigroup $\mathcal M _L = \mathfrak{F_{is}} (E)/{\sim_L}$ by the ideal generated by all the elements of the form $(e^{-1}f)^\downarrow$, for distinct $e,f\in X$, $X\in C$, it follows from Proposition \ref{prop:Toeplitz-Munn-EUtrees} and the above observation that $ \mathcal{LI} (E,C)$ is a strongly $E^*$-unitary semigroup, with an idempotent pure partial homomorphism $\pi \colon \mathcal{LI} (E,C)^\times \to \mathbb F$. The result now follows from \cite[Proposition 2.1]{ABC25} and Proposition \ref{prop:Toeplitz-Munn-EUtrees}.

\label{def:reduced-paths}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph, and let $C^{\mathrm{fin}}$ denote the subset of $C$ consisting of elements $X\in C$ such that $|X|<\infty$. We define a {\it choice function} as a function $\mathfrak E\colon C^{\mathrm{fin}} \to E^1$ such that $\mathfrak E (X) \in X$ for all $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$.
We say that $\lambda \in \mathbb F_{C}$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced if it does not end with $\mathfrak E (X)$ for any $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} $. 

	  We say that an element $T\in \mathcal X _0$ is {\it $\mathfrak E$-reduced} if each maximal element of $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced. Note that, if $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced, then $T\in \mathcal X_L$, because the maximal elements of $T$ do not end in an edge $e$ of $E$ such that $\{e\}\in C$.

label: thm:basis-forLabneutralcomp
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that the set of idempotents $\{\mathbf{e} (T) : T \text{ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced} \}$ is a $K$-basis for $\mathcal L_1$.    
	
	Set $e_X:= \mathfrak E (X)\in X$ for all $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. 
	
	We apply Bergman's Diamond's Lemma for commutative algebras \cite{Bergman-Diamond}, see especially \cite[Theorem 1.2 and Section 10.3]{Bergman-Diamond}. We define $\text{wt}(e_X)= 2$ and $\text{wt}(x)= 1$ for any other $x\in E^1\cup E^{-1}$. We consider a weight  function on $\mathbb F_{C}$ such that the weight of $\lambda \in \mathbb F_{C}$ is the sum of the weights of the edges of $\lambda$, or $\text{wt}(\lambda) = 1$ if $\lambda = v\in E^0$. We extend this weight function to the free commutative semigroup $W:= [\mathbb F_{C} ]$ generated by $\mathbb F_{C}$ by declaring the weight of a monomial $\lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_r$ as the sum of the weights $\text{wt}(\lambda_i)$, $i=1,\dots, r$.  
	
	For $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, set $X':= X \setminus \{e_X\}$. 
	
	We now consider the following reduction system $\mathcal S$ on the semigroup algebra $\operatorname{\mathrm{Pol}}_K[\mathbb F_{C}] = KW$: 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $(\lambda \cdot \mu , 0)$ if $\lambda,\mu\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and $s(\lambda)\ne s(\mu)$. 
		\item $(\lambda \cdot \mu ,  \lambda )$ if $\lambda,\mu\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and $\mu \le_p \lambda$,
		\item $(\lambda \cdot \mu , 0)$ if $\lambda $ and $\mu$ are $C$-incompatible, where $\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb F_{C}$.
		\item $(\lambda e^{-1},  \lambda) $ where $\lambda e^{-1}\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and $e\in E^1$.
		\item $(\lambda e_X, \lambda - \sum_{e\in X'} \lambda e)$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$ and $\lambda e_X \in \mathbb F_{C}$.  
	\end{enumerate}	 
	
	Observe that the reduction system $\mathcal S'$ consisting of the pairs in (1)--(4) leads to the basis of $\mathcal C$ consisting of idempotents in Scheiblich normal form. 
	
	Define a partial order $\le $ on $W=[\mathbb F_{C}]$ by
	$$\lambda \le \mu \iff \lambda = \mu \text{ or } \text{wt}(\lambda)	< \text{wt} (\mu).$$
	Then the partial order $\le $ on $W$ is a semigroup partial order compatible with the reduction system $\mathcal S$. Moreover $\le$ satisfies the descending chain condition. In order to apply the Diamond Lemma, we have to check that all ambiguities are resolvable. 
	We leave to the reader to check that all ambiguities involving pairs (1)--(4) are resolvable.
	We will check those concerning reduction pairs of the family (5), which are necessarily inclusion ambiguities with either (2) or (3). 
	
	Suppose we have an element of the form $\lambda e_X \cdot \mu$ such that $\mu \le_p \lambda e_X$. Then we have an inclusion ambiguity
	$$\lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(2)}{\to} \lambda e_X, \qquad \lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(5)}\to \lambda \cdot \mu  - \sum_{e\in X'} \lambda e \cdot \mu.$$
	Applying (5) to the first, we get
	$$ \lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(2)}{\to} \lambda e_X \overset{(5)}{\to} \lambda - \sum_{e\in X'} \lambda e.$$
	We now distinguish two cases. If $\mu \le _p \lambda$ then we have
	$$\lambda \cdot \mu - \sum _{e\in X'} \lambda e \cdot \mu \overset{(2)}{\to} \lambda - \sum _{e\in X'} \lambda e ,$$
	and we have solved the ambiguity. If $\mu = \lambda e_X$, then 
	$$\lambda \cdot \lambda e_X - \sum _{e\in X'} \lambda e \cdot \lambda e_X \overset{(2)}{\to} \lambda e_X - \sum _{e\in X'} \lambda e \cdot \lambda e_X \overset{(3)}{\to} \lambda e_X ,$$
	and we have solved the ambiguity too.
	
	If $\lambda e_X \le_p \mu$, then we can solve the corresponding inclusion ambiguity for $\lambda e_X \cdot \mu$ just as in the case where $\mu = \lambda e_X$.  
	
	Finally we consider inclusion ambiguities involving (3) and (5). Suppose that 
	$\lambda e_X$ and $\mu$ are $C$-incompatible. If $\lambda $ and $\mu $ are already $C$-incompatible then we have
	$$ \lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(2)}{\to}  0, \quad \lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(5)}{\to} \lambda \cdot \mu - \sum_{e\in X'} \lambda e \cdot \mu \overset{(2)}{\to} 0-0 = 0.$$
	If $\mu = \lambda e \mu'$, where $e\in X'$, then 
	$$ \lambda e_X \cdot \mu \overset{(5)}{\to} \lambda \cdot \lambda e \mu'  - \sum_{f\in X'} \lambda f \cdot \lambda e \mu' \overset{(2),(3)}{\longrightarrow} 
	\lambda e \mu' - \lambda e \cdot \lambda e \mu' \overset{(2)}{\to} \mu - \mu = 0.$$
	
	The irreducible forms are precisely the elements which correspond to the family $\overline{\mathcal B}_1(E,C)$, that is, the elements
	$$\lambda _1\cdots \lambda_r ,$$
	where $\lambda _i $ does not end in $E^{-1}$, does not end in $e_X$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, and $\lambda_1,\cdots ,\lambda _r$ is an incomparable $C$-compatible family of elements of $\mathbb F_{C} (v)$, for some $v\in E^0$. 
	
	Hence we obtain the desired result for the neutral component.

title: Proof
body_md:
We work within $\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C)$, where we have a natural linear basis, namely $\mathcal{S} (E,C)$, whose elements admit a unique normal form, the Scheiblich normal form \cite[Theorem 4.6]{ABC25}. For $g\in \mathbb F_{C}(v)\setminus \{v\}$, the ideal $\mathcal C_g$ of $\mathcal C$ is the linear span of the elements $\mathbf{e} (T)$, where $T\in \mathcal X_0 (v)$ and $g_0\in T$, and the component $\mathcal C_g\rtimes g$ is the linear span in $\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C)$ of corresponding terms $\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$. 
	
	
	A {\it monomial} in $\mathcal C =\mathcal C_1$ is an element of the form 
$\lambda_1 \lambda_1^* \lambda_2 \lambda_2^* \cdots \lambda _r \lambda_r^*$, where $\lambda_i \in \mathbb F_{C}$. 
	It follows from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:basis-forLabneutralcomp} that 	
every element of $\mathcal C $, written as a linear combination of monomials, can be transformed, using the reductions (1)--(5) applied to these monomials, to a linear combination of monomials in $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich form, that is, monomials of the form $\mathbf{e} (T)$ for $T$ a $\mathfrak E$-reduced $C$-compatible $E$-tree. Moreover this linear combination does not depend on the particular reductions that we use. We denote the $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form of $a\in \mathcal C$ by $n(a)$. Of course $n$ is linear: $n(\sum \alpha_i a_i) = \sum \alpha_i n(a_i)$, where $\alpha_i$ are scalars and $a_i \in \mathcal C $.
	
	Now if $g\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and  $a\in \mathcal C_{g}$ there is no guarantee that $n(a) \in \mathcal C_{g_L}$. We define
	$$n^g(a) = n(a) g_Lg_L^*,$$
	and we call $n^g(a)$ the $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form of $a$ relative to $g$. Note that $n^g$ is linear on $\mathcal C_g$.
	
	Since $a\in \mathcal C_g = gg^* \mathcal C _1$, and $g_Lg_L^* gg^*= gg^*$ we have $ag_Lg_L^* = a$, hence
	$$a-n^g(a) = g_Lg_L^*(a-n(a)) \in  g_Lg_L^* \mathcal Q_1 = \mathcal Q_{g_L}.$$
	In particular $a$ and $n^g(a)$ represent the same element of $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$. 
	
	Moreover it is clear that $n^g(a)$ is a linear combination of monomials in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form relatively to $g_L$.
	
	We want to show that $n^g(a)$ is the unique linear combination of monomials in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form relatively to $g_L$ that represents $a$. Let $\sum \alpha _i a_i$ be a linear combination of monomials $a_i$ which are in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form relatively to $g_L$ and such that $\sum \alpha_i a_i$ represents $a$.
	
	Suppose that we can prove that $n^{g} (a_i)=a_i$ for all $i$. We will show then that $n^g(a) = \sum \alpha_i a_i$. 
	For, observe that since $a$ and $\sum \alpha_ia_i$ represent the same element of $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$, we have
	$$n(a) = n(\sum \alpha_i a_i) = \sum \alpha _i n(a_i).$$
	Therefore 
	$$n^g(a) = g_Lg_L^* n(a) = \sum \alpha _i g_Lg_L^* n(a_i) = \sum \alpha_i n^{g} (a_i) = \sum \alpha _i a_i,$$
	where in the last step we have used that $n^{g} (a_i) = a_i$ for all $i$.
	
	Hence we only need to show that $n^{g}(a) = a$ for each monomial $a$ in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form relatively to $g_L$. Let $a$ be one of such monomials, and write $a= \mathbf{e} (T)$ for $T\in \mathcal X_L$. We can assume that $g_L\in \mathrm{max} (T)$ and that $g_L$ is not $\mathfrak E$-reduced. 
	Set $A= \mathrm{max}(T)\setminus \{g_L\}$.
	Write 
	$$g_L = g_1 w_1 e_{X_1}\cdots w_r e_{X_r},$$ where $X_i\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, each $w_i$ is either trivial or a product of elements of the form $x^*$ for $x\in E^1$, and either $g_1\in A^{\downarrow}$ and $g_1w_1e_{X_1}\notin A^{\downarrow}$, or $g_1\notin A^{\downarrow}$ and $g_1$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced. Set $X'= X\setminus \{e_X\}$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. In either case we have
	$$n(a) = \mathbf{e} ((\{g_1\} \cup A)^{\downarrow}) - \sum _{i=1}^r \sum _{e\in X_i'} \mathbf{e} ( (\{g_1 w_1 e_{X_1} \cdots w_ie\}\cup A)^{\downarrow}). $$
	Now observe that 
	$$g_Lg_L^* \mathbf{e} ((\{g_1\} \cup A)^{\downarrow}) = 
	\mathbf{e} ( (\{g_L\}\cup A)^{\downarrow}) = a$$
	and that for all $i\in \{ 1,\dots , r\}$ and $e\in X_i'$
	$$g_Lg_L^*\mathbf{e} ( (\{g_1w_1e_{X_1}\cdots w_ie\}\cup A)^{\downarrow}) = 0, $$
	because $g_L$ and $g_1w_1e_{X_1}\cdots w_ie$ are $C$-incompatible. We conclude that 
	$$n^g(a) = [g_Lg_L^* n(a)]= a,$$
	as desired. 
	
	Hence all elements of $\mathcal L _g \rtimes g$ have a unique representative which is a linear combination of monomials in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form relatively to $g_L$, and we conclude that $\overline{\mathcal B}(E,C)$ is a linear basis of $\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$.

label: exam:non-separated-case
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exam:non-separated-case}
We observe here that, in the non-separated case, the basis $\overline{\mathcal B}(E,C)$ from Theorem \ref{thm:full-basis-forLab} is closely related to the basis given in \cite[Theorem 1]{zel} (see also \cite[Corollary 1.5.12]{AAS}). Indeed, we show below that these two bases are essentially connected through the Scheiblich normal form. This gives further evidence that this is the appropriate basis for $\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$.


Suppose that $a= \lambda \mu^*$ is a basis element in the Cohn path algebra $\mathcal C_K(E)$ of a non-separated graph $E$, with $r(\lambda ) = r(\mu)$. Then we write 
$$\lambda = \lambda_1 \lambda_2, \qquad \mu = \mu_1 \lambda _2,$$
where $\lambda_1$ and $\mu_1$ do not end with the same edge.
Now $\lambda _1\mu_1^{-1}\in \mathbb F_{C}$ is a reduced word, and
$$a= \lambda \mu^* =\lambda_1 \lambda_2 \lambda_2^* \mu_1^* = \lambda _1(\lambda _2\lambda_2^*)(\lambda_1^*\lambda_1)\mu_1^* = (\lambda \lambda^*) (\lambda_1 \mu_1^*) ,$$
so that the Scheiblich normal form of $a$ is precisely 
$$a= (\lambda\lambda^*)(\lambda_1\mu_1^*).$$

Let $\mathfrak E$ be a choice function for $E$, that is, for each regular vertex $v$ of $E$, we have  $e_v:= \mathfrak E (v)\in s^{-1}(v)$. 

	Suppose that $a=\lambda \mu^*$ is in $\mathfrak E$-reduced form with respect to a choice function $\mathfrak E$, in the sense of \cite{zel}. This means that  the expression $\lambda\mu^*$ does not contain the subword $e_ve_v^*$, for regular vertices $v$ in $E$.
	
	 Suppose first that $\lambda_2$ in the above decomposition is non-trivial. Then, with $g:= \lambda_1\mu_1^{-1}\in \mathbb F_{C}$, $\mathbf{e} (\lambda) \rtimes g$ is in $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form, and we clearly have $g_L <_p \lambda$. 
	 
	 Conversely, if $a=\mathbf{e} (\lambda) \rtimes g $  is in $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form and $g_L <_p \lambda$, then we can write $g= g_L x_1\cdots x_r \mu^{-1}$ in reduced form in $\mathbb F_{C}$, where $s^{-1}(s(x_i)) = \{ x_i\}$ for $i=1,\dots , r$, $r\ge 0$, and moreover $\lambda$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced in the sense of Definition \ref{def:reduced-paths}. It follows that $\lambda = g_L x_1\cdots x_r \lambda _2$ for a non-trivial $\mathfrak E$-reduced path $\lambda_2$, and we get
	 \begin{align*}
	 a= & \mathbf{e} (\lambda )\rtimes g= g_L x_1\cdots x_r \lambda_2 \lambda _2^* x_r^*\cdots x_1^* g_L^* g_L x_1\cdots x_r \mu^* \\
	  =  & g_L x_1\cdots x_r \lambda _2 \lambda _2 ^* \mu^* = (\lambda_1\lambda _2) (\mu \lambda_2)^*,
	 \end{align*}
	 where $\lambda _1 = g_Lx_1\cdots x_r$, and $a= \lambda (\mu \lambda_2)^*= (\lambda_1\lambda _2)(\mu \lambda_2)^*$ is the $\mathfrak E$-reduced normal form of $a$ in the sense of \cite{zel}.  
	 
	 Suppose now that $\lambda _2$ is trivial. Then $g := \lambda \mu^{-1}$ is already a reduced word in $\mathbb F_{C}$, and the $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form of $a$ is $ \mathbf{e} (g_L) \rtimes g$, where $\lambda = g_L x_1\cdots x_r$, with $s^{-1}(s(x_i))= \{x_i\}$ for all $i$ and $r\ge0$. In this case, $g_L$ may be or may not be $\mathfrak E$-reduced in the sense of Definition \ref{def:reduced-paths}, but in any case 
	 $\mathbf{e} (g_L)\rtimes g$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_L$. Conversely, if we have a (reduced) element $g= \lambda \mu^{-1}$ in $\mathbb F_{C}$, then $\mathbf{e}(g_L)\rtimes g$ is the $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form of $\lambda \mu^*$, and $\lambda \mu^* $ is its $\mathfrak E$-reduced normal form in the sense of \cite{zel}. Incidentally, note that both normal forms do not depend on the choice function $\mathfrak E$ in the case where $\lambda_2$ is trivial.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:total-length}
	Let $T$ be a non-trivial $E$-tree and let $hx\in \mathrm{max} (T)$, where $x\in \hat{E}^1$. Then $T\setminus \{hx\}$ is also an $E$-tree, and $|T\setminus \{hx\}| = |T|-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It is clear that removing a maximal element of a tree will produce another tree. The formula $|T\setminus \{hx\}| = |T|-1$ is also clear because $T\setminus \{hx\}$ has exactly one edge less than $T$, namely the edge $(h,hx)$.

label: thm:semigroup-generated
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:semigroup-generated} Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Then
	the natural homomorphism $\iota \colon \mathcal{LI} (E,C)\to \mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$ is injective. Hence the semigroup of $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$ generated by $E^0\cup E^1\cup (E^1)^*$ is naturally isomorphic to the Leavitt inverse semigroup $\mathcal{LI} (E,C)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will use the picture of $\mathcal{LI} (E,C)$ established in Theorem \ref{thm:ECLeavittMunntrees}. 
	With this picture, we have $\iota ((T,g)) = \mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$ for any Leavitt-Munn $(E,C)$-tree $(T,g)$. 
	We fix a choice function $\mathfrak E\colon C^{\mathrm{fin}}\to E^1$ for $(E,C)$. 
	
	
	Let $(T,g)$ be a Leavitt-Munn $(E,C)$-tree. Then $T\in \mathcal X_L$ and $g_L\in T$. Set $A := \mathrm{max} (T) \setminus \{g_L\}$, and $B := \{ g \in A : g \text{ is not } \mathfrak E\text{-reduced}\, \}$.  
	If $B=\emptyset$, then $\mathbf{e} (T) \rtimes g$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_L$, so that $\iota ((T,g))= \mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g \in \overline{\mathcal B}(E,C)$

If $B\ne \emptyset$, 
	write $B= \{h_1e_{X_1},\dots , h_r e_{X_r}\}$, where $X_i\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_{r(h_i)}$ and $|X_i| \ge 2$ for $i=1,\dots , r$. Set $X'=X\setminus \{e_X\}$ for any $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$ with $|X|\ge 2$. 
	

	Using the relation $r(h_1)= e_{X_1}e_{X_1}^* + \sum _{x\in X_1'} xx^*$, we can write in $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$
$$\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g = - \sum_{x\in X_1'} \mathbf{e} ((T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\})\cup \{h_1x\}\}))\rtimes g + \mathbf{e} (T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\}))\rtimes g.$$
By Lemma \ref{lem:total-length}, $|T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\}| = |T| -1$, and observe that 
$$| (T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\})\cup \{h_1x\} | = |T|$$
and that $\mathrm{max}((T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\})\cup \{h_1x\})\setminus \{g_L\} = (A \setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\})\cup \{h_1x\}$, for each $x\in X_1'$. On the other hand, the $E$-tree $T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\}$ is obviously $C$-compatible, but it does not necessarily belong to $\mathcal X_0$ or $\mathcal X_L$. However its reduction to a tree in $\mathcal X_L$, namely $(T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1}\})_L$, will have total length strictly less than $|T|$.

For $(x_1,\dots ,x_r)\in X'_1\times \cdots \times X'_r$, set
$$T_{(x_1,\dots , x_r)} = (T\setminus \{h_1e_{X_1},\dots , h_re_{X_r}\})\cup \{h_1x_1,\dots ,h_rx_r\}.$$
Also, set $U:= \mathfrak E (C^{\mathrm{fin}}) = \{ e_X : X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}\}$, and observe that the set of edges $e\in E^1$ such that $s^{-1}(s(e)) = \{ e\}$ is a subset of $U$. Let $T_U$ be the $U$-reduction of $T$, as in Lemma \ref{lem:uniqueTU}.  

Iterating the above process a finite number of times, we obtain an identity
in $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$ of the form
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:ng-reduction}
\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g = (-1)^r \sum_{(x_i)\in \prod_{i=1}^r X_i'} \mathbf{e} (T_{(x_i)})\rtimes g + \tau + \mathbf{e} (T_U\cup g_L^\downarrow)\rtimes g ,	
\end{equation}
  where $\tau$ is a linear combination of terms of the form $\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g\in \overline{\mathcal B} (E,C)$ such that $$|T_U\cup g_L^\downarrow | < |S| < |T_{(x_i)}| = |T|$$
  for all $(x_i)\in \prod_{i=1} ^r X_i'$. Observe that \eqref{eq:ng-reduction} gives the $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal form of $\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$, since all $T_{(x_i)}$ and also $T_U\cup g_L^\downarrow$ are $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_L$. 
  
  We are now ready to show the injectivity of $\iota$. Suppose that $\iota ((T,g)) = \iota ((T',h))$ for Leavitt-Munn $(E,C)$-trees $(T,g)$ and $(T',h)$. Since these are homogeneous elements of degree $g$ and $h$ respectively, we must have $g=h$. Let $A'$ and $B'$ be the sets as above corresponding to $T'$. Set
  $B'= \{h_1'e_{Y_1},\dots , h_s' e_{Y_s}\}$, where $Y_j\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_{r(h_i')}$ and $|Y_j| \ge 2$ for $j=1,\dots , s$. We have a formula similar to \eqref{eq:ng-reduction} for $T'$, involving the $\mathfrak E$-reduced
  relatively to $g_L$ trees $T'_{(y_1,\dots , y_s)}$ for $(y_j)\in \prod_{j=1}^s Y_j'$, and $T'_U\cup g_L^\downarrow$. 
  
  Since $\mathbf{e}(T)\rtimes g = \mathbf{e} (T')\rtimes g$ in $\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$, it follows that their $\mathfrak E$-reduced Scheiblich normal forms are equal. 
  Looking at the highest length terms and the lowest length terms of the developments of $\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$ and $\mathbf{e} (T')\rtimes g$ in \eqref{eq:ng-reduction}, we conclude that 
  \begin{equation}
  	\label{eq:highest-terms}
  	 (-1)^r \sum_{(x_i)\in \prod_{i=1}^r X_i'} \mathbf{e} (T_{(x_i)}) =  (-1)^s \sum_{(y_j)\in \prod_{j=1}^s Y_j'} \mathbf{e} (T'_{(y_j)})  
  \end{equation}     
and $T_U\cup g_L^\downarrow = T'_U\cup g_L^\downarrow$. We claim that $A\setminus B= A'\setminus B'$. 
By symmetry, it suffices to check one of the inclusions. Let $g\in A\setminus B$. Then obviously $g\notin B'$. We want to check that $g\in A'$. Looking for a contradiction, suppose that $g\notin A'$. Then by
\eqref{eq:highest-terms} there is $j\in \{1,\dots ,s\}$ and $y\in Y_j'$ such that $g=h_j'y$. But since $g\in A= \mathrm{max} (T)\setminus \{g_L\}$, and $g$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced, it follows that $g\in \mathrm{max} (T_U)$. Hence, using that $T_U\cup g_L^\downarrow = T'_U\cup g_L^\downarrow$, we get $g=h_j'y\in T'_U$, which is a contradiction, since $T'_U$ does not contain any path of the form $h_j'z$, for $z\in Y_j$. This shows that 
$A\setminus B = A'\setminus B'$. It is now easy to see, by using again \eqref{eq:highest-terms}, that $B=B'$.
Indeed, assume that $g=h_{i_0}e_{X_{i_0}}\in B$ and fix an edge $x\in X_{i_0}'$. Then $h_{i_0}x$ is a maximal element in some 
of the the trees $T_{(x_i)}$ and so, by \eqref{eq:highest-terms}, it must be a maximal element in some of the trees $T'_{(y_j)}$. If $h_{i_0}x\in A'\setminus B'$, then $h_{i_0}x\in A\setminus B$, but then 
$h_{i_0}x,h_{i_0}e_{X_{i_0}}\in T$, which is impossible, because $T$ is $C$-compatible. Hence $h_{i_0}x\notin A'\setminus B'$, and it follows that there is $j_0\in \{ 1,\dots ,s\}$ and $y\in Y'_{j_0}$ such that $h_{i_0}x = h_{j_0}'y$, which implies that $h_{i_0}=h_{j_0}'$ and $x=y$. In particular, $X_{i_0}=Y_{j_0}$ and thus
$$g= h_{i_0}e_{X_{i_0}} = h'_{j_0}e_{Y_{j_0}} \in B'.$$
Hence $B\subseteq B'$ and similarly $B'\subseteq B$. Since $A\setminus B = A'\setminus B'$ and $B=B'$, we get $A=A'$ and thus $(T,g)=(T',g)= (T',h)$, as desired. 


This concludes the proof.

label: def:Sreduced-paths
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Sreduced-paths}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and let $S$ be a subset of $C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. 
	We define a {\it $S$-choice function} as a function $\mathfrak E\colon S \to E^1$ such that $\mathfrak E (X) \in X$ for all $X\in S$.
	We say that $\lambda \in \mathbb F_{C}$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced if it does not end with $e_X$ for all $X\in S$. 
	
	We say that an element $T\in \mathcal X _0$ is {\it $\mathfrak E$-reduced} if each maximal element of $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced. 
	
	Let $g\in \mathbb F_{C}$. 
	We say that $T\in D_g^S$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_S$ if each element in $\mathrm{max} (T)\setminus \{ g_S\}$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced. That is, if either $g_S$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced or $g_S$ is not maximal in $T$, then $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_S$ if and only if $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced, and if $g_S$ is not $\mathfrak E$-reduced and $g_S$ is maximal in $T$, then $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_S$ if and only if all maximal elements of $T$ except $g_S$ are $\mathfrak E$-reduced.

\label{thm:full-basis-forCLS}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph, and let $S$ be a subset of $C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, and let $\mathfrak E$ be an $S$-choice function for $(E,C)$. Then a linear basis 
	of $CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S)$ is given by the elements of the form 
	$$\overline{\mathcal B} (E,C,S) :=\{ \mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g : T \in D_g^S \text{ and } T \text{ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_S$} \}.$$

label: prop:relationLPACPA
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:relationLPACPA}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and $S$ a subset of $C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. Let $p:= \sum_{v\in E^0} v\in \mathcal M (\mathcal L_K (E_S,C^S))$. Then we have a natural $*$-isomorphism
	$$\varphi\colon CL_K (E,C,S) \cong p\mathcal L _K (E_S,C^S)p$$
	such that $\varphi (v)= v$ for all $v\in E^0$ and $\varphi (e)= e$ for all $e\in E^1$. 
	
	In particular $\mathcal C_K (E,C) \cong p\mathcal L _K (\overline{E},\overline{C}) p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have a natural $*$-homomorphism $\varphi \colon CL_K (E,C,S) \to p \mathcal L_K (E_S,C^S) p$ defined by $\varphi (v)= v$ and $\varphi (e)= e$ for all $v\in E^0$ and $e\in E^1$. Note that $R:=p\mathcal L _K (E_S,C^S)p$ is generated as $*$-algebra by $E^0\cup E^1$ together with the projections $d_Xd_X^*$, for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S$, with the Cohn path algebra relations amongst the elements of $E^0\cup E^1$, the Leavitt path algebra relations $v=\sum _{e\in X} ee^*$ for all $X\in S$, and the additional relations that $d_Xd_X^*$ is a projection, and that
	$$v = \sum _{e\in X} ee^* +d_Xd_X^*$$
	for each $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_v\setminus S$, $v\in E^0$. 
	Note that these relations automatically imply that $e^*d_Xd_X^* = 0=d_Xd_X^* e$ for all $e\in X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S$ and that $d_Xd_X^*\le v$ whenever $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_v \setminus S$. 
	Note that $\varphi (q_X) = d_Xd_X^*$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S$.
	
	We can define a map $\psi \colon p\mathcal L_K(E_S,C^S)p\to CL_K(E,C,S)$ by 
	$\psi (v)= v$, $\psi (e)= e$ for $v\in E^0$ and $e\in E^1$, and $\psi (d_Xd_X^*)= q_X = v-\sum_{e\in X} ee^*$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_v\setminus S$. Using the above observations, we see that this map preserves all the relations amongst the generators of $p\mathcal L_K(E_S,C^S)p$, and hence induces a $*$-homomorphism which is clearly the inverse of $\varphi$. 
	This completes the proof.

label: thm:relationLPACPA-TAME
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:relationLPACPA-TAME}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and $S$ a subset of $C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. Let $p:= \sum_{v\in E^0} v\in \mathcal M (\mathcal L_K (E_S,C^S))$. Then we have a natural $*$-isomorphism
$$\overline{\varphi} \colon CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S) \cong p\mathcal L _K^\mathrm{ab} (E_S,C^S)p$$
such that $\overline{\varphi} (v) = v$ for all $v\in  E^0$ and $\overline{\varphi} (e) = e$ for all $e\in E^1$.  
	
	In particular, $\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C) \cong p \mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C}) p$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Observe that the $*$-homomorphism $\varphi$ from Proposition \ref{prop:relationLPACPA} induces a surjective
	$*$-homomorphism $\overline{\varphi} \colon  CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S) \twoheadrightarrow p\mathcal L _K^\mathrm{ab} (E_S,C^S)p$.
	To show that it is injective, we prove that $\overline{\varphi}$ sends a basis of  $CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S)$ to 
	a linearly independent family in  $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E_S,C^S)$. Let $\mathfrak E$ be a $S$-choice function for $(E,C)$. This means that we have a map $\mathfrak E\colon S\to E^1$ such that $\mathfrak E (X) \in X$ for all $X\in S$. We extend $\mathfrak E$ to a choice function $\overline{\mathfrak E} \colon (C^S)^{\text{fin}} \to E_S^1$ by letting $\overline{\mathfrak E} (X) = \mathfrak E (X) \in X$ for each $\overline{X} = X \in S$ and $\overline{\mathfrak E} (\overline{X}) = d_X \in \overline{X} = X\cup \{d_X\}$ for all $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} \setminus S$.  
	
	We consider the basis $\mathcal B := \overline{\mathcal B}_{\mathfrak E} (E,C,S)$ of $CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S)$ given in Theorem \ref{thm:full-basis-forCLS} with respect to the $S$-choice function $\mathfrak E$, and the basis
	$\overline{\mathcal B} := \overline{\mathcal B}_{\overline{\mathfrak E}} (E_S,C^S)$ of $\mathcal L _K^\mathrm{ab} (E_S,C^S)$ with respect to the choice function $\overline{\mathfrak E}$ given in Theorem \ref{thm:full-basis-forLab}. If $\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$ is an element of the basis $\mathcal B$, then $g_S\in T$ and $T$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_S$. But then, since neither of the edges of $g$ and neither of the edges of $T$ are of the forms $d_X$ or $d_X^{-1}$ for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} \setminus S$, we see that $g_L = g_S$ and that $T$ is $\overline{\mathfrak E}$-reduced relatively to $g_L$. Here $g_L$ is computed with respect to the separated graph $(E_S,C^S)$, and we remark that $|\overline{X}|\ge 2$ for all $\overline{X}\in C^S\setminus S$. Hence $\mathbf{e} (T)\rtimes g$ belongs to the basis $\overline{\mathcal B}$. Hence $\overline{\varphi}$ restricts to an injective map from the basis $\mathcal B$ of $CL_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C,S)$ into the basis 
	$\overline{\mathcal B}$ of $\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E_S,C^S)$, as desired.

label: cor:lfbipartite

body_md:

title: Definition
body_md:
\cite[Definition 4.3]{ABC25}
	\label{def:idempotents-IsetminusF}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and let $T\in \mathcal X_0$. 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The idempotent $\mathbf{e} (T)$ associated to $T$ is 
		$$\mathbf{e} (T) = \prod _{\lambda\in \mathrm{max} (T)} \lambda \lambda^*.$$ 
		\item Suppose now that $\lambda \in \mathcal N (T)$. Then there is a unique decomposition $\lambda = \lambda_0\lambda_1$, where $\lambda_0\in T$, $\lambda_1= x_1^{-1}\cdots x_r^{-1}y$, $r\ge 0$, $x_1,\dots , x_r,y\in E^1$ and $\lambda_0[x_1^{-1}\cdots x_r^{-1}y]_1\notin T$. Define
		$$\mathbf{e} (\lambda_0\setminus \lambda) = \lambda_0\lambda_0^*-\lambda \lambda^* = \lambda_0 (r(\lambda_0) - \lambda_1\lambda_1^*)\lambda_0^* \in \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C).$$
		\item For a finite subset $F$ of $\mathcal N (T)$, define the idempotent $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$ as follows: 		
		$$\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F) = \mathbf{e} (T)\cdot \prod_{\lambda_0\lambda_1\in F} \mathbf{e}(\lambda_0\setminus \lambda_0 \lambda_1) = \prod _{\lambda_0\lambda_1\in F} \mathbf{e} (T\setminus \{\lambda_0\lambda_1\}).$$
		\item For $v\in E^0$ and $e\in s^{-1}(v)$ we define
		$$\mathbf{e} (v\setminus e) = v-ee^*.$$
		\item For $v\in E^0$ and $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_v$, define
		$$q_X = \mathbf{e} (v\setminus X) = \prod_{e\in X} \mathbf{e} (v\setminus e) = v - \sum_{e\in X} ee^* \in \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C).$$
	\end{enumerate}

label: def:blocking family
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:blocking family}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and $T\in \mathcal X_0$. A {\it blocking family} for $T$ consists of a finite subset $F$ of $\mathcal N (T)$, where
	$$F= \bigsqcup_{i=1}^r \gamma_0^i(\gamma_1^i X_i)$$
	where $\gamma_0^i\in T$, and $\gamma_0^i\gamma_1^iX_i = \{ \gamma_0^i\gamma_1^ix : x\in X_i \}$ for $X_i \in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_{r(\gamma_0^i\gamma_1^i)}$, with $\gamma^i x = (\gamma_0^i)(\gamma_1^i x)$ being the standard form of the element $\gamma^i x\in \mathcal N (T)$, as described in Definition \ref{def:idempotents-IsetminusF}(2).
	
	We say that a blocking family $F$ is {\it prime} if it consists of a single set, that is if $F= \gamma X$ for a single $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. Observe that 
	$$\mathbf{e} \Big(T \setminus \big(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^r \gamma_0^i(\gamma_1^i X_i)  \big)\Big) = \prod_{i=1}^r \mathbf{e} (T\setminus \gamma_0^i\gamma_1^iX_i) .$$

label: lem:keyforbasis-of-L
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:keyforbasis-of-L}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Consider the set
	$$\mathcal B'' = \{ \mathbf{e} (T\setminus F) \rtimes g : T\in \mathcal X _0, [T]\in D_g \text{ and } F=\gamma X \text{ is a prime blocking family for } T\}. $$
	Then $\mathcal Q$ is the $K$-linear span of $\mathcal B''$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is enough to prove that for $\mathbf{e}(I) \rtimes g, \mathbf{e} (J)\rtimes h \in \mathcal{S}(E,C)$, the element 
	$$(\mathbf{e} (I)\rtimes g)q_X(\mathbf{e} (J) \rtimes h)$$ is in the $K$-span of $\mathcal B''$.
	We may assume that this product is nonzero. In this case we have $r(g) = v$, where $X\in C_v$, and thus we have
	$$ (\mathbf{e} (I)\rtimes g) q_X= \mathbf{e}(I\setminus gX) \rtimes g.$$
	Now writing $((gg^{-1})\rtimes g)(\mathbf{e} (J)\rtimes h) = \mathbf{e} (J')\rtimes (g\cdot h)$ for some $J'\in \mathcal X_0$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lem:key-for-keyforbasis-of-L}:
	$$(\mathbf{e} (I)\rtimes g)q_X(\mathbf{e} (J) \rtimes h) = (\mathbf{e}(I\setminus gX)e(J'))\rtimes (g\cdot h) = \mathbf{e} ((I\cup J')\setminus gX) \rtimes (g\cdot h)\in \mathcal B''.$$

label: rmk:noĺinearly-independent
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:noĺinearly-independent}
	The generating family $\mathcal B''$ of $\mathcal Q$ given in Lemma \ref{lem:keyforbasis-of-L} is not linearly independent in general. We show this with an example. Let $(E,C)$ be the Cuntz separated graph, with $|C| >1$, let $a,b$ be two distinct edges of $E$ and set $E^0=\{v\}$. Let $A=\{a\}$ and $B=\{b\}$. Then we have
	$$\mathbf{e} (A\setminus B) = aa^*- aa^* bb^*,\qquad \mathbf{e} (B\setminus A) = bb^*-aa^* bb^*.$$
	Hence we obtain the following non-trivial linear relation for the distinct elements $\mathbf{e}(A\setminus B), \mathbf{e}(B\setminus A), \mathbf{e}(v\setminus A), \mathbf{e}(v\setminus B)$:
	$$\mathbf{e} (A\setminus B) + \mathbf{e} (v\setminus A) = \mathbf{e}(B\setminus A) + \mathbf{e}(v\setminus B).$$

label: lem:blocking-are-different
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:blocking-are-different}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph, $I,J\in \mathcal X_0$, $F$ a blocking family for $I$, and $G$ a blocking family for $J$. If $\mathbf{e}(I\setminus F) = \mathbf{e} (J\setminus G)$, then $I=J$ and $F=G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\overline{\varphi}(\mathbf{e} (I\setminus F)) = \mathbf{e} (T)$ and $\overline{\varphi}(\mathbf{e}( J\setminus G)) = \mathbf{e} (T')$, where $T,T'\in \mathcal X_L (\overline{E},\overline{C})$, and $\overline{\varphi}$ is the isomorphism established in Theorem \ref{thm:relationLPACPA-TAME}. Here 
 	$$T= I\cup \{\gamma_1d_{X_1},\dots , \gamma_r d_{X_r}\}^\downarrow ,$$
 	where $F= \bigsqcup _{i=1}^r \gamma_i X_i$, and similarly with $T'$. 
 		Since $\mathbf{e} (T)= \mathbf{e} (T')$ we get $T=T'$ by Theorems \ref{thm:semigroup-generated} and \ref{thm:ECLeavittMunntrees}. So it suffices to notice that $I$ and $F$ can be recovered from $T$. Indeed $I = S_0$, where $S$ is the tree given by
 	$$S = T\setminus  \{ \gamma d_X : \gamma d_X \in T\},$$
 	and then $F$ is the blocking family $\{\gamma X : \gamma d_X\in T\}$ for $I=S_0$.

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:key-basis-for-Q}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and let $\mathfrak E \colon C^{\mathrm{fin}} \to E^1$ be a choice function for $(E,C)$. The {\it canonical $\mathfrak E$-basis of $\mathcal Q$} is the set $\mathcal B (\mathcal Q) $ consisting of all elements of the form $\mathbf{e}(T\setminus F)\rtimes g$, where $T\in \mathcal X_0$, $F$ is a non-empty blocking family for $T$, $g_0\in T$, and $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_0$.

label: thm:BQ-basis-ofQ
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:BQ-basis-ofQ}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and $\mathfrak E$ a choice function for $(E,C)$. Then the canonical $\mathfrak E$-basis $\mathcal B (\mathcal Q)$ is a linear basis of $\mathcal Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Observe first that, for $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g\in \mathcal B (\mathcal Q)$, we have $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\in \mathcal Q$, because $F$ is a non-empty blocking family for $T$, and thus $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g \in \mathcal Q$. 
	
	
	Now let $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$ be the separated graph associated to $(E,C)$, so that we have a $*$-isomorphism $\overline{\varphi} \colon \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C) \to p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})p$ by Theorem \ref{thm:relationLPACPA-TAME}. Recall that $\overline{E}^0=E^0 \sqcup \{v_X: X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} \}$, $\overline{E}^1 = E^1\sqcup \{ d_X: X \in C^{\mathrm{fin}} \}$, and $\overline{C}_v = \{\overline{X}: X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}_v \}\sqcup C^{\mathrm{inf}}_v$, where $\overline{X}= X \sqcup \{ d_X\}$ for each $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} $ and $C^{\mathrm{inf}} = \{X\in C : |X|=\infty\}$. We define a choice function 
	$\widetilde{\mathfrak E}\colon \overline{C}^{\text{fin}} \to \overline{E}^1$ for $(\overline{E}, \overline{C})$ by
	$$\widetilde{\mathfrak E}(\overline{X}) = \mathfrak E (X) \in E^1 .$$
	Let $\overline{\mathcal B} := \overline{\mathcal B}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak E}} (\overline{E}, \overline{C})$ be the linear basis of $\mathcal L _K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})$ associated to the choice function $\widetilde{\mathfrak E}$, see Theorem \ref{thm:full-basis-forLab}. The elements of $\overline{\mathcal B}$ are of the form $\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g$, where  $S\in D_g^{\overline{L}}$ is $\widetilde{\mathfrak E}$-reduced relatively to $g_{\overline{L}}$, and $g\in \mathbb F _{\overline{C}}$. Note that the edges $d_X$ are terminal, in the sense that any path $\gamma \in \mathbb F_{\overline{C}}$ such that $s(\gamma )\in E^0$ and ending in $d_X$ for some $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$ cannot be properly extended to a path in $\mathbb F_{\overline{C}}$ . 
	
	Set $\overline{\mathcal Q}:= \overline{\varphi} (\mathcal Q) \subset p\mathcal L_K^{\mathrm{ab}} (\overline{E}, \overline{C}) p$. By the previous observation, any basis element $\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes  g \in \overline{\mathcal B}\cap p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})p$ satisfies that $g\in \mathbb F_{C}$, that is, $g$ cannot contain any edge of the form $d_X$, for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. 
	It follows that a basis of $\overline{\mathcal Q}$ is given by all the elements 
	$\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g \in \overline{\mathcal B}$ such that $S$ contains some path of the form $hd_X$, for some $h\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and some $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, and $g\in \mathbb F_{C}$. Note that these paths $hd_X$ are necessarily maximal in $S$, since they cannot be properly extended. We denote this basis of $\overline{\mathcal Q}$ by $\mathcal B (\overline{\mathcal Q})$     	
	  
	  In order to complete the proof, we have to check that $\overline{\varphi} (\mathcal B (\mathcal Q)) = \mathcal B (\overline{\mathcal Q})$. Suppose first that $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g\in \mathcal B (\mathcal Q)$. Then $T\in \mathcal X_0$, $F= \bigsqcup_{i=1}^r \gamma^0_i(\gamma^1_i X_i) $ is a non-empty
	  blocking family for $T$, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:blocking family}, $g_0\in T$, and all non-$F$-blocked maximal elements of $T$, except possibly $g_0$, are $\mathfrak E$-reduced.  Now observe that 
	 $\overline{\varphi} (\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g) = \mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g$,
	  where 
	  $$\mathrm{max} (S) = \text{NB-max} (T\setminus F) \bigsqcup  \{ \gamma_i^0\gamma _i^1 d_{X_i} : i=1,\dots , r\}.$$
	  On the other hand, since $|\overline{X}| \ge 2$ for all $\overline{X}\in \overline{C}^{\text{fin}}$, we have $g_{\overline{L}} = g_0$ for all $g\in \mathbb F_{C}$, so that $g_{\overline{L}} \in S$. Since  
	  $$\mathrm{max} (S)\setminus \{g_{\overline{L}}\} = (\text{NB-max} (T) \setminus \{g_0\}) \bigsqcup  \{ \gamma_i^0\gamma _i^1 d_{X_i} : i=1,\dots , r\}$$
	and $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_0$, it follows that $S$ is $\widetilde{\mathfrak E}$-reduced relatively to $g_{\overline{L}}= g_0$. Moreover $r\ge 1$ because $F$ is non-empty, so we conclude that $\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g\in \mathcal B (\overline{\mathcal Q})$. 
	
	Conversely, suppose that $\mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g \in \mathcal B (\overline{\mathcal Q})$. We can write
	$\mathrm{max} (S) = M_1 \sqcup M_2$, where $M_1$ are the maximal elements of $S$ which end in $E^1$ and $M_2$ are the maximal elements of $S$ which end in $d_X$ for some $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$. We can write
	$$M_2 = \{ \gamma_i d_{X_i} : i=1,\dots , r\},$$
	where $\gamma_i\in \mathbb F_{C}$ and $X_i\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, for $i=1,\dots ,r$. 
	
	Set $S' := S\setminus M_2$, and note that $S'\in \mathcal X (= \mathcal X (E))$, because no path in $S'$ involves the edges $d_X$, for $X\in C^{\mathrm{fin}} $. Now let 
	$$A:= \mathrm{max} \{ h_0 : h\in S'\}  \quad  \text{ and } \quad T= A^\downarrow .$$
	Then $T\in \mathcal X_0$, and $T\subseteq S'\subseteq S$. We now will define a suitable blocking family $F$ for $T$. Take an element $\gamma_i d_{X_i}\in M_2$. We can write $\gamma_i = \gamma_i^0 \gamma_i^1$ where $\gamma^0_i$ is a maximal prefix of $\gamma_i$  with the property $\gamma^0_i\in T$. Note that $\gamma_i^1$ might be trivial. Define
	$$F:= \bigsqcup_{i=1}^r \gamma_i^0 (\gamma_i^1 X_i).$$
	We claim that $F$ is a blocking family for $T$. The only thing we need to check for this is that 
	$F\cap T= \emptyset$. Suppose that $\gamma_i^0\gamma_i^1 x\in T$ for some $x\in X_i$. If $\gamma_i^1$ is non-trivial, this cannot happen, so we may assume that $\gamma_i^1$ is trivial. In this case, $\gamma _i x \in S$ because $T\subseteq S$, and also $\gamma_i d_{X_i}\in S$, with $x,d_{X_i} \in \overline{X}_i$, which is impossible because $S$ is $\overline{C}$-compatible. Hence we obtain that $F$ is a blocking family for $T$. Moreover $g_0 = g_{\overline{L}} \in S'$ and thus $g_0\in T$ by the  definition of $T$.  
	
	We now check that $\text{NB-max} (T\setminus F) = M_1$. By construction we have $M_1\subseteq \text{NB-max} (T\setminus F)$. Suppose that $\gamma \in \text{NB-max} (T\setminus F)$. In particular, $\gamma \in \mathrm{max} (T)$, and since $T\subseteq S$, we can extend $\gamma $ to a maximal element $h$ of $S$. If $h\in M_1$, then 
	$h\in T$ and thus $\gamma = h\in M_1$ by maximality of $\gamma$ in $T$. If $h\in M_2$ then
	$\gamma \le_p \gamma_i^0 \gamma_i^1 d_{X_i}$ for some $i\in \{ 1,\dots, r\}$.  But since $\gamma\in \mathrm{max} (T)$, it follows that $\gamma = \gamma _i^0$, which implies that $\gamma \in \text{B-max} (T\setminus F)$, in contradiction with our assumption. We have therefore shown that $\text{NB-max} (T\setminus F) = M_1$.
	Since $S$ is $\widetilde{\mathfrak E}$-reduced relatively to $g_0$, it follows that $ \mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$ is $\mathfrak E$-reduced relatively to $g_0$. It follows that $\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g \in \mathcal B (\mathcal Q)$. 
    
    Finally we show that $\overline{\varphi} (\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g)= \mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g$. By the first part of the proof we have
    $$\overline{\varphi} (\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g)= \mathbf{e} (S'')\rtimes g ,$$
    where $\mathrm{max} (S'') = \text{NB-max} (T\setminus F) \bigsqcup \{ \gamma_i d_{X_i}: i=1\dots , r\}$ and since
    $\text{NB-max} (T\setminus F) = M_1$, we get $\mathrm{max} (S'') = M_1\sqcup M_2 = \mathrm{max} (S)$, which shows that
    $S= S''$. Hence  $\overline{\varphi} (\mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)\rtimes g)= \mathbf{e} (S)\rtimes g$, as desired. 
    This completes the proof.

label: rem:Ruy-consonant-semigroups
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Ruy-consonant-semigroups}
The notion of consonant inverse semigroups has been recently introduced by Exel \cite{exel2025}. Roughly, two inverse semigroups are consonant if they have the same tight groupoid, see \cite[Theorem 9.5]{exel2025} for the precise statement. Here we notice that the natural surjection $\pi \colon \mathcal{S} (E,C) \to \mathcal{LI} (E,C)$ is a consonance for every separated graph $(E,C)$. 

Let $S$ be an inverse semigroup and let 
$\Delta \colon S \to  \text{Bis}^{\text{oc}}(\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight}(S))$ 
be the natural map defined in \cite{exel2025}, 
where $\text{Bis}^{\text{oc}}(\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight}(S))$ is the inverse semigroup of open compact bisections of the tight groupoid $\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (S)$ of $S$. Then there is a natural injective semigroup homomorphism  $U \mapsto 1_U$ from  
$B:= \text{Bis}^{\text{oc}}(\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight}(S))$ to the multiplicative semigroup of the Steinberg algebra $A_K (\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (S))$.
Hence we may identify $B$ with an inverse subsemigroup of the multiplicative semigroup of $A_K (\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (S))$. 
In particular $\Delta (S)$ is identified with an inverse subsemigroup of $A_K (\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (S))$.

Now let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph and let $S := \mathcal{S}(E,C)$ be the inverse semigroup of the separated graph $(E,C)$. By 
Theorem \ref{thm:structure-of-Leavitt} there is a natural  $*$-isomorphism $\mathcal L^\mathrm{ab}_K (E,C) \cong A_K (\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (S))$.
Under this isomorphism, $\Delta (S)$ corresponds to the natural image of $S$ in $\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C)$, which is the subsemigroup of 
$\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab}(E,C)$ generated by $E^0 \cup E^1 \cup  (E^1)^*$. But now by Theorem \ref{thm:semigroup-generated}, 
this semigroup is isomorphic to $\mathcal{LI} (E,C)$. Hence there is an isomorphism $\overline{\Delta}\colon  \mathcal{LI}(E,C) \to \Delta (S)$ such that $\overline{\Delta} \circ \pi = \Delta$.
Since, by \cite[Proposition 8.11]{exel2025}, $\Delta \colon  S \to  \Delta (S)$ is a consonance, so is $\pi \colon  \mathcal{S}(E,C) \to \mathcal{LI}(E,C)$.

label: thm:new-groupoid-model

body_md:
\label{thm:new-groupoid-model}
		Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Then there is an isomorphism of groupoids
		$$\mathcal G _\mathrm{tight} (E,C) := \mathcal G_\mathrm{tight} (\mathcal{S}(E,C)) \cong \mathfrak T_L \rtimes \mathbb F.$$
		Moreover 
		$$\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C) \cong A_K ( \mathfrak T_L \rtimes \mathbb F) \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathcal O  (E,C) \cong C^* (\mathfrak T_L\rtimes \mathbb F).$$

label: lem:well-defined-inverse-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:well-defined-inverse-product}
The inverse and product in $\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (E,C)$ given above are well defined, and correspond to the groupoid   structure on the tight groupoid of $(E,C)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first check that the inverse is well-defined, that is, for $(Z',g,Z)\in \mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (E,C)$, we have
	   	that $(Z,g^{-1},Z')\in \mathcal{G}_\mathrm{tight} (E,C)$. By definition, $Z\in \mathfrak F_L$, $(g^{-1})_L\in Z$, and
	   	$Z'= [g\cdot Z \cup g^\downarrow]_L$. Hence we see that $g_L\in Z'$. 
	   	
	   	We claim that $Z'\cup g^\downarrow = g\cdot Z$. Indeed, it is clear that $Z'\cup g^\downarrow =
	   	(g\cdot Z \cup g^\downarrow)_L \cup g^\downarrow $ is contained in $g\cdot Z$. Now let $z\in Z$. We can write $g=x_1\cdots x_r x_{r+1}\cdots x_n$, $z= x_n^{-1}\cdots x_{r+1}^{-1}y_1\cdots y_m$ in reduced form, where $m\ge 0$ and $y_1\ne x_r$ if $m\ge 1$. If $m=0$ then $g\cdot z = x_1\cdots x_r \in g^\downarrow \subseteq  [g\cdot Z \cup g^\downarrow]_L \cup g^\downarrow $. If $m\ge 1$, then 
	   	$g\cdot z = x_1\cdots x_r y_1\cdots y_m$, and  since $Z\in \mathfrak F_L$, there exists $y_{m+1},\dots ,y_{m+k}\in E^1\cup E^{-1}$, with $k\ge 0$, such that 
	   	$$x_n^{-1} \cdots x_{r+1}^{-1}y_1\cdots y_my_{m+1} \cdots y_{m+k} \in Z \quad \text{ and } \quad y_{m+k}\in X\in C^{>1},$$
	   	and it follows that $x_1\cdots x_r y_1\cdots y_{m+k} \in (g\cdot Z)_L$ and thus that $g\cdot z \in (g\cdot Z)_L$, because $(g\cdot Z)_L$ is a lower set. Therefore $g\cdot z \in (g\cdot Z \cup g^\downarrow)_L \cup g^\downarrow $ also in this case. 
	   	
	   	 We now check that the product is well-defined. Let $(Z_1',g_1,Z_1), (Z_2',g_2,Z_2)$ be two triples such that $Z_1= Z_2'$. We know that $(g_1^{-1})_L \in Z_1$ and that $(g_2)_L\in Z_2'= Z_1$. Hence assuming that $Z_1\in \mathfrak F_L(v)$, we get
	   	 $$s(g_2) = s((g_2)_L)= v = s((g_1^{-1})_L) = r(g_1) ,$$
	   	 so that $s(g_2)= r(g_1)$. Hence $g_1\cdot g_2$ is at least in $\mathfrak{F_{gr}} (E)$. Hence, to show that 
	   	 $g_1\cdot g_2 $ belongs to $\mathbb F_{C}$, it suffices to show that $g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1}$ belongs to $\mathbb F_{C}$, which in turn is equivalent to check that $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L \in \mathbb F_{C}$.  
	   	 
	   	We will check that  $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L \in Z_2$, which in particular implies that  $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L \in \mathbb F_{C}$. Write $g_2 = x_1\cdots x_n$ and $g_1 = y_1\cdots y_t x_r^{-1} \cdots x_1^{-1}$ in reduced form, with $y_t\ne x_r$, $y_t\ne x_{r+1}^{-1}$, $0\le r\le n$, and $x_i,y_j\in E^1\cup E^{-1}$. We then have
	   	$g_1\cdot g_2 = y_1\cdots y_t x_{r+1} \cdots x_n$, and 
	   	$$(g_1\cdot g_2)^{-1} = g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1} = x_n^{-1} \cdots x_{r+1}^{-1} y_t^{-1} \cdots y_1^{-1}.$$   
	   	 
	   	 We distinguish two cases:
	   	 \begin{enumerate}
	   	 	\item $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L = x_n^{-1}\cdots x_{r+1}^{-1}y_t^{-1}\cdots y_i^{-1}$, with $i \le t$.
	   	 	\item $(g_2^{-1} \cdot g_1^{-1})_L = x_n^{-1}\cdots x_j^{-1}$, with $j\ge r+1$. 
	   	 \end{enumerate}
	   	 
	   	 If (2) happens, then $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L \le_p (g_2^{-1})_L \in Z_2$ and thus $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L\in Z_2$. If (1) holds, then $(g_1^{-1})_L = x_1\cdots x_r y_t^{-1}\cdots y_i^{-1}$ and since
	   	 $$(g_1^{-1})_L \in Z_1 = Z_2' = g_2\cdot Z_2 \cup g_2^\downarrow ,$$
	   	 we get 
	   	 $$(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L =  x_n^{-1}\cdots x_{r+1}^{-1}y_t^{-1}\cdots y_i^{-1} = g_2^{-1}\cdot (g_1^{-1})_L \in g_2^{-1}\cdot (g_2\cdot Z_2 \cup g_2^\downarrow ) = Z_2\cup (g_2^{-1})^\downarrow .$$
	   	  If $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L\in Z_2$, we are done. Otherwise we have $(g_2^{-1}\cdot g_1^{-1})_L\in (g_2^{-1})^\downarrow$, which is impossible since $x_{r}\ne y_t$. 
	   	 
	   	 
	   	Now we check that $[(g_1\cdot g_2)\cdot Z_2 \cup (g_1\cdot g_2)^\downarrow ]_L = Z_1'$.  Indeed we have
	   	\begin{align*}
	   		g_1\cdot Z_1 \cup g_1^\downarrow & = g_1\cdot (g_2\cdot Z_2 \cup g_2^\downarrow) \cup g_1^\downarrow \\
	   		& = (g_1\cdot g_2) \cdot Z_2 \cup g_1\cdot g_2^\downarrow \cup g_1^\downarrow \\ 
	   		& = (g_1\cdot g_2) \cdot Z_2 \cup (g_1\cdot g_2)^\downarrow \cup g_1^\downarrow .
	   		   	\end{align*}
	   	  	   	Hence $Z_1'= [g_1\cdot Z_1 \cup g_1^\downarrow]_L = [(g_1\cdot g_2) \cdot Z_2 \cup (g_1\cdot g_2)^\downarrow \cup g_1^\downarrow]_L$, and it suffices to show that $(g_1)_L \subseteq  
	   	  	   	(g_1\cdot g_2) \cdot Z_2 \cup (g_1\cdot g_2)^\downarrow$. Suppose first that $(g_1)_L= y_1\cdots y_l$ for some $l\le t$. Then we have
	   	  	   	$$(g_1)_L = y_1\cdots y_l \le_p (g_1\cdot g_2)_L .$$
	   	  	   	Assume now that $(g_1)_L = y_1\cdots y_t x_r^{-1}\cdots x_s^{-1}$ for some $s\le r$.  Then $x_n^{-1} \cdots x_{r+1}^{-1}x_r^{-1}\cdots x_s^{-1} = (g_2^{-1})_L$, and hence
	   	  	   	$$(g_1)_L = (y_1\cdots y_tx_{r+1}\cdots x_n)\cdot (x_n^{-1}\cdots x_s^{-1}) = (g_1\cdot g_2)\cdot (g_2^{-1})_L \in (g_1\cdot g_2)\cdot Z_2.$$
	   	  	   	Hence $(g_1)_L\in (g_1\cdot g_2)\cdot Z_2$ in this case. 
	   	  	   	
	   	  	   	
	   	  	   	Finally, it is easily seen that this structure agrees with the groupoid structure of $\mathfrak T_L\rtimes \mathbb F$, which by Theorem \ref{thm:new-groupoid-model} is isomorphic to $\mathcal G_\mathrm{tight} (E,C)$. This concludes the proof.

We denote by $\Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}$ the set of Leavitt $(E,C)$-trees which do not admit an exit, and we denote by $\Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}_0$ the subset of $\Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}$ of those Leavitt $(E,C)$-trees $T$ such that there is no closed path $\alpha = \beta \gamma \beta^{-1}$, where $\gamma $ is a cycle, $(\alpha^{-1})_L \in T$ and $(\alpha\cdot T \cup \alpha^\downarrow)_L = T$. label: prop:isoand-isoiso-forOmega
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:isoand-isoiso-forOmega}
	Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. Then the set of isolated points of $\Omega (E,C)$ coincides with the set $\Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}$ of all (finite) Leavitt $(E,C)$-trees which do not admit exits. Moreover the set $\Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}_0$ is the set of isolated points $z\in \Omega (E,C)$ with trivial isotropy.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $Z$ is an isolated point in $\Omega (E,C) = \mathfrak T _L$. Then by Theorem \ref{thm:new-charac-tight-spectrum}, $Z$ is an element in $\mathfrak F_L$ with no finite exits.  Moreover, there is an open set of the form $V:=\mathcal Z_L (T\setminus F) \cap \mathfrak T_L$, where $T\in \mathcal X_L$ (that is, $T$ is a Leavitt $(E,C)$-tree), and $F$ a finite subset of $\mathcal N ^{\mathrm{inf}}_L (T)$, such that $V= \{Z\}$. But if $T$ admits an exit, then we can build at least two different elements $Z_1,Z_2\in \mathcal Z_L (T\setminus F)$, which then can be extended to two different elements $Z_1',Z_2'\in \mathcal Z_L (T\setminus F) \cap \mathfrak T _L$, and we get a contradiction. It follows that $T$ has no exits, and then again by Theorem \ref{thm:new-charac-tight-spectrum}, $T\in \Omega (E,C)$. Moreover $F=\emptyset$, because $T$ has no infinite exits. It follows that $Z=T$ is a Leavitt $(E,C)$-tree without exits. 
	
	Conversely, if $T$ is a Leavitt $(E,C)$-tree without exits, then $T\in \Omega (E,C)$ and $\mathcal Z_L (T) = \{T\}$, and so $T$ is an isolated point in $\Omega (E,C)$. 
	
	The last statement follows from Lemma \ref{lem:trivial-properties-isotropy}.

title: Proof
body_md:
If some of the edges of $g'$ is positively oriented, then we would obtain an exit of $T$, because $|X|\ge 2$ for all $X\in C$. Hence all edges of $g'$ are inverse edges. Let $e^{-1}$ be one of these edges, and suppose that $e\in X\in  C_{s(e)}$. We then have $gg''e^{-1} \le_p h$ for some initial segment $g''$ of $g'$. If there is $Y\in C_{s(e)}$ such that $X\ne Y$, then choosing $y\in Y$, we obtain an exit $gg''e^{-1}y$ of $T$, which is a contradiction. Hence $|C_{s(e)}| = 1$.   
	
	
	
	We now show that the isotropy group at $T$ is trivial. Suppose, by way of contradiction that $\alpha \in F_{T}$ is a non-trivial element in the isotropy group of $T$. By Lemma \ref{lem:trivial-properties-isotropy}, we have $\alpha = \beta \gamma \beta^{-1}$, where $\gamma $ is a cycle. Moreover $\alpha ^n = \beta \gamma^n \beta^{-1}$ is also an element in $F_{T}$ for all $n\in \mathbb Z$, by Lemma \ref{lem:trivial-properties-isotropy}. Replacing $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{-1}$ if needed, we may assume that $\gamma$ contains an edge $e\in E^1$. In particular, $\beta \gamma^{n-1} \gamma _L = \beta \gamma^{n-1} \gamma_0 \le _p (\alpha^n)_L$ for all $n>0$, and thus the lengths of the paths $(\alpha^n)_L$ are unbounded. Since $(\alpha^n)_L\in T$ for all $n$, and $T$ is a finite tree, this is impossible, and thus we get a contradiction. Hence $F_T$ is trivial, and so $T\in \Omega^{\mathrm{iso}}_0$.

label: def:completely-blocked
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:completely-blocked} Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph, and let 
	$T\in \mathcal X_0$. We say that $T$ {\it can be completely blocked} if $\mathcal N (T)$ is finite and non-empty. This implies that for any element $\gamma_0\gamma_1 y\in \mathcal N(T)$, we have $y\in Y\in C^{\mathrm{fin}}$, and that there is a maximum blocking family $F=\sqcup _{i=1}^r \gamma_0^i(\gamma_1^iX_i)$ for $T$, which contains all the elements of $\mathcal N (T)$.
	We denote by $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$ the idempotent given by
	$\mathbf{ecb} (T) = \mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$, where $F$ is the maximum blocking family for $T$. The set of elements $T\in \mathcal X_0$ which can be completely blocked will be denoted by $\mathcal X_{\mathrm cb}$.
head: environment

label: thm:completelyblocked
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:completelyblocked} Let $(E,C)$ be a separated graph. 
	For each $T\in \mathcal X_{\mathrm cb}$, the idempotent $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$ belongs to $\mathcal Q \cap \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C))$. Moreover,  $\mathcal Q \cap \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C))$ is the ideal of $\mathcal C_K ^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)$
	generated by all the idempotents $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$, for $T\in \mathcal X_{\mathrm cb}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First observe that $\mathbf{ecb} (T)= \mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$ belongs to the ideal $\mathcal Q$, because $\mathcal N (T)$ is non-empty and finite. 
	
	
	Let $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$ be the separated graph associated to $(E,C)$. Any $T\in \mathcal X_0$ can be considered also as a $\overline{C}$-compatible tree in $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$. Moreover $T\in \overline{\mathcal X}_L$, that is, $T$ belongs to the set $\mathcal X_L(\overline{E},\overline{C})$, so the concept of an exit has been defined for $T$ with respect to $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$. By the isomorphism  $\mathcal C^\mathrm{ab} _K(E,C)\cong p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})p$, the idempotent $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$ corresponds to $\mathbf{e} (T')$, for the Leavitt $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$-tree $T'$, where 
	$$T' = T\cup \big( \bigcup_{i=1}^r \{ \gamma^i_0 \gamma^i_1 d_{X_i} \}^\downarrow \Big),$$
	with $F= \sqcup _{i=1}^r  \gamma_0^i(\gamma_1^iX_i)$ the maximum blocking family for $T$. It follows that $T'$ has no exits in $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$, so that $T'$ is an isolated point in $\Omega (\overline{E},\overline{C})$ by Proposition \ref{prop:isoand-isoiso-forOmega}.

Since $|\overline{X}| \ge 2$ for all $\overline{X}\in \overline{C}$, it follows from Lemma \ref{lem:isotropy-when-all-groups-havemoreon-element} that $\Omega^{\text{iso}} (\overline{E},\overline{C}) = \Omega^{\text{iso}}_0 (\overline{E},\overline{C})$, hence $T'\in \Omega^{\text{iso}}_0 (\overline{E},\overline{C})$ and $\mathbf{e} (T')\in \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C}))$ by Theorem \ref{thm:socle-tameLeav-algebra}.

Hence we get 
	$$\mathbf{e} (T') \in p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})p\cap \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})) = \mathrm{soc} (p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})p) \cong \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C)),$$
	and thus $\mathbf{ecb} (T) \in  \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C))\cap \mathcal Q$, as claimed. 
	       
	      Finally, suppose that $e$ is a minimal idempotent in $\mathcal Q$.
	      
	      
	       Let $\overline{\varphi}\colon \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C) \to p\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} ({E},\overline{C})p$ be the isomorphism from Theorem \ref{thm:relationLPACPA-TAME}, and set $\overline{\mathcal Q} = \overline{\varphi} (\mathcal Q)$. 
	        Then $\overline{\varphi} (e)$ is a minimal idempotent in the ideal 
	        $p\,  \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})) p\cap \overline{\mathcal Q}$ of $p \mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})  p$. 
	        Now observe that 
	        $$p\, \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C})) p \cong \bigoplus_{[T]\in \overline{\Omega}^{\text{iso}}_0/{\mathcal R}} M_{\delta (T)}(K),$$
	        	where $\delta (T)$ is the number of elements in the orbit of $T$ which belong to $\overline{\mathcal X}_L(v)$, for some $v\in E^0$. Indeed a system of matrix units for the component 
	        	$M_{\delta(T)}(K)$ is given by the elements $e_{\alpha,\beta}$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:socle-tameLeav-algebra}, where $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb F_{C}(v)$ for some $v\in E^0$. 
	       It follows that there exists some $T'\in \overline{\Omega}^{\text{iso}}_0$ such that $T'\in \overline{\mathcal X}_L (v)$ for some $v\in E^0$ and 
	       $\overline{\varphi} (e)\sim \mathbf{e} (T')$ within $p\, \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{E},\overline{C}))p$.
	       Now let 
	       $$T'':= T'\setminus \{ \gamma d_X : \gamma d_X\in T' \},$$
	       which is a tree in $\mathcal X(v)$ and set $T= (T'')_0 \in \mathcal X_0(v)$. Then $\mathcal N (T)$ is finite because $T'$ has no exits with respect to $(\overline{E},\overline{C})$, and $\overline{\varphi} (\mathbf{ecb} (T)) = \mathbf{e} (T')$. It follows that       
	       $e\sim \mathbf{ecb}(T)$ within $\mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E,C))$. In particular, $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$ is a minimal idempotent in $\mathcal Q$. 
	        
	       
	       It remains to check that $\mathcal N (T)$ is non-empty. Set  $f := \mathbf{ecb} (T)= \mathbf{e} (T\setminus F)$, where $F$ is the maximum blocking family for $T$. We have to show that $F\ne \emptyset$.      
	      	      Since $f\in \mathcal Q$, it follows from Theorem \ref{thm:BQ-basis-ofQ} that we can write \begin{equation}
	      	      	\label{eq:equality-for-f}
	      	      	f= \sum_{i=1}^r \lambda_i \mathbf{e} (T_i\setminus F_i),
	      	      \end{equation} 
	      	      where $\lambda_i\in K^\times$ and $F_i$ is a non-empty blocking family for $T_i\in \mathcal X_0$, $i=1,\dots , r$. We may assume that 
	      	      $f\mathbf{e} (T_i\setminus F_i)\ne 0$ for all $i$. 
	      	            	     With this assumption, we then have 
	      $f = f\mathbf{e}(T_i\setminus F_i)$ by the minimality of $f$. Hence multiplying the relation \eqref{eq:equality-for-f} by $\prod_{i=1} ^r \mathbf{e} (T_i\setminus F_i)$ we get
	      $$ f= (\sum_{i=1}^r \lambda_i)  \prod_{i=1} ^r \mathbf{e} (T_i\setminus F_i).$$
	      Hence $f=  \prod_{i=1} ^r \mathbf{e} (T_i\setminus F_i) = \mathbf{e} \Big( (\cup_{i=1}^r T_i)\setminus (\cup_{i=1}^r F_i)\Big)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:key-for-keyforbasis-of-L}, and thus $T= \cup_{i=1}^r T_i$, $F= \cup_{i=1}^r F_i \ne \emptyset $, by Lemma \ref{lem:blocking-are-different}. Hence $F\ne \emptyset$, and the proof is complete.

\label{exam:Q-for-nonseparated}
	If $E$ is a non-separated graph, the structure of the ideal $\mathcal Q$ is transparent, see \cite[Propositions 1.5.8 and 1.5.11]{AAS}. Each regular vertex $v$ gives rise to an idempotent $q_v = v -\sum_{e\in s^{-1}(v)} ee^*\in \mathcal Q$, and we have $\mathcal Q\subseteq \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K (E))$. The idempotents $q_v$ determine the different homogeneous components of $\mathcal Q$. These facts are no longer true for a separated graph, in which case the situation is much more involved, as we will see in the following examples. Note that, in the above situation, $\{v\}$ can be completely blocked, and $\mathbf{ecb} (v) = q_v$.

\label{rem:Bavula}
	Although $\mathrm{soc} (\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E_X,C)) = 0$ when $|X|>1$, one may find a related algebra which has a nonzero socle, by imposing some extra commuting relations. Indeed Bavula introduced in \cite{bavula} the algebra $\mathbb S_n$ as the algebra generated by $x_1,\dots ,x_n,y_1,\dots ,y_n$ with the defining relations
	$$y_1x_1= \cdots = y_nx_n=1, \quad [x_i,x_j] = [y_i,y_j] = [x_i,y_j] = 0 \, \text{ for all } i\ne j.$$
	Clearly $\mathbb S_n$ is a quotient algebra of $\mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (E_{X_n},C)$, where $X_n= \{ x_1,\dots ,x_n\}$. 
	By \cite[Proposition 4.1]{bavula}, the socle of $\mathbb S_n$ is a simple, essential ideal of $\mathbb S_n$.

label: exam:free-inverse-monoid
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exam:free-inverse-monoid}
Let $X$ be any non-empty set. The free inverse monoid $\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)$ is realized in \cite[Examples 3.4 and 4.10]{ABC25} as a corner of the inverse semigroup of a certain separated graph $(F_X, D)$, as follows.  
Let $F_X$ be the graph with $F_X^0 = \{ v\} \sqcup X$ and $F_X^1 = \{e_x,f_x : x\in X \}$, with $s(e_x) = s(f_x) = v$ and $r(e_x) = r(f_x) = x$ for all $x\in X$.
We take the free separation $D$ on $F_X$, so that $D_v = \{\{ e_x\},\{f_x\} : x\in X\}$ and $D_x= \emptyset$ for all $x\in X$. Then by \cite[Example 4.10]{ABC25} we have a (unique) monoid isomorphism $\varphi\colon \mathfrak{F_{im}} (X) \to v\mathcal{S} (F_X,D) v$ such that $\varphi (x)= e_xf_x^{-1}$ for all $x\in X$. Consequently, we get a $*$-isomorphism 
$$\varphi \colon K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)] \to v\cdot \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (F_X,D)\cdot v$$
and so we can apply the theory of separated graphs to study the monoid algebra $K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]$. 
It was shown in \cite[Proposition 4.5]{AG17} that, in the case where $|X|= 1$, the socle of $K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]$ is isomorphic to $\bigoplus _{i=1}^\infty M_i(K)$, and it is an essential ideal of $K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]$. 


We can now generalize this result for any set $X$, as follows. The bipartite separated graph $(\overline{F_X}, \overline{D})$ consists in adding sinks $v_x, v_x'$ and edges $d_x,d_x'$ to $F_X$, for each $x\in X$, such that $s(d_x)= s(d_x')= v$, $r(d_x)=v_x$, $r(d_x')= v_x'$, and 
$$\overline{D}_v = \{ \{e_x,d_x\}, \{f_x,d_x'\} : x\in X\}.$$
Note that $d_xd_x^* = v-e_xe_x^*$ corresponds to $1-xx^*$ and $d_x'(d_x')^*$ corresponds to $1-x^*x$ under the isomorphism 
$$v\cdot \mathcal L_K^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{F_X},\overline{D})\cdot v \cong v\cdot  \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (F_X,D)\cdot v \cong K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]$$
obtained from  Corollary \ref{cor:lfbipartite} and \cite[Example 4.10]{ABC25}. 

As shown in \cite[Example 4.10]{ABC25}, each $T\in \mathcal X_0$ corresponds uniquely with an ordinary finite tree $T$, containing $1$, in the Cayley graph of the free group $\mathbb F$ on $X$.
We will refer to such a tree simply as a finite tree, and we will denote the set of finite trees by $\mathfrak M$. The elements of $\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)$ correspond to Munn trees $(T,g)$, where $T\in \mathfrak M$ and $g\in T$, see for instance \cite[Section 6.4]{lawson}. 

Given a finite tree $T\in \mathfrak M$, we define the {\it neighborhood} $\mathcal N (T)$ of $T$ as the set of all the elements $\gamma z \in \mathbb F$, where $\gamma \in T$, $z\in X\cup X^{-1}$, and $\gamma z \notin T$. In other words the set $\mathcal N (T)$ of {\it neighbors} of $T$ is the set of words which are at distance $1$ of $T$. Hence $\mathcal N (T)$ is always non-empty, and it is finite if and only if $X$ is finite. We say that $\gamma \in T$ is an {\it interior point} of $T$ if all the reduced words $\gamma z$, $z\in X\cup X^{-1}$, belong to $T$. Of course $T$ does not have interior points when $X$ is infinite. If $ \gamma z\in \mathcal N (T)$, we say that $\gamma z$ is a neighbor of $T$ at $\gamma \in T$.  



Define an equivalence relation $\sim $ on the set $\mathfrak M$ of finite trees $T$ over $X$ by declaring that $T\sim S$ if and only if $S= g\cdot T$, where $g^{-1}\in T$. 

Suppose that $X$ is finite, and take $T\in \mathfrak M$. Then the idempotent $\mathbf{ecb} (T)$ corresponds to the evaluation $\mathbf{e} (T')$, where $T'$ is the tree obtained by adding to $T$ maximal elements $\gamma d_x$ for each $\gamma x \in \mathcal N(T)$, and $\gamma d'_x$ for each $\gamma x^{-1}\in \mathcal N (T)$, for each $x\in X$. Moreover, by Proposition \ref{prop:finite-orbits}, we have
$$\mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{F_X},\overline{D})) \cong \bigoplus _{[T]\in \mathfrak M /\sim} M_{|T'|} (K).$$
Hence we get
$$\mathrm{soc} (K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]) = p\cdot \mathrm{soc} (\mathcal L_K ^\mathrm{ab} (\overline{F_X},\overline{D}))\cdot p \cong \bigoplus _{[T]\in \mathfrak M /\sim} M_{|T|} (K).$$
 
 In conclusion, we obtain the following result for $K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]\cong v\cdot \mathcal C_K^\mathrm{ab} (F_X,D) \cdot v$:
 
 $$\mathrm{soc} (K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]) \cong \begin{cases}
 	\bigoplus _{[T]\in \mathfrak M /{\sim}} M_{|T|} (K) & \text{ if } |X| <\infty \\
 	\qquad \qquad 0 & \text{ if } |X| = \infty .
 	\end{cases}$$
 It is also easy to show that $\mathrm{soc} (K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)])$ is essential in $K[\mathfrak{F_{im}} (X)]$ when $X$ is finite.

body_md:
We have to show that $B_iB_j\subseteq B_{i+j}$ for all $i,j\in \mathbb Z^+$.
  	Suppose that $T_1\setminus F_1$ has $i+1$ exits and $T_2\setminus F_2$ has $j+1$ exits, and that $T_1\cap F_2 = T_2\cap F_1= \emptyset$. We have to show that $(T_1\cup T_2)\setminus (F_1\cup F_2)$ has $\le i+j+1$ exits. If $T_1= T_2$, then 
  	$$\mathcal N (T_1\cup T_2) -|F_1\cup F_2| \le  |\mathcal N (T_1)| -|F_1| \le i+1 \le i+j+1,$$
  	because $j\ge 0$. If $T_1\nsubseteq T_2$, take $\gamma \in T_1\setminus T_2$. Then $\gamma = \gamma _1 z \gamma_2$, where $\gamma _1 \in T_2$, $ \gamma _1 z\notin T_2$ and $z\in X\cup X^{-1}$, so that $\gamma _1 z \in \mathcal N (T_2)$ and $\gamma _1 z \notin F_2$ since $T_1\cap F_2 = \emptyset$.  
  	Now observe that
  	$$\mathcal N (T_1\cup T_2)\setminus (F_1\cup F_2 ) \subseteq (\mathcal N (T_1)\setminus F_1) \cup ((\mathcal N (T_2)\setminus F_2)\setminus \{\gamma_1 z\}),$$
  	hence $|\mathcal N (T_1\cup T_2)\setminus (F_1\cup F_2)| \le (i+1) + (j+1-1) = i+j+1$, and thus $(T_1\cup T_2)\setminus (F_1\cup F_2)$ has $\le i+j+1$ exits. By symmetry, the same inequality holds if $T_2\nsubseteq T_1$.
